newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia strike cuts road freight - transporters.
newsitem.headline: Colombia strike cuts road freight - transporters.

text.p: Road freight in Colombia has dropped by as much as 30 percent as a result of the public sector strike which entered its second day Wednesday, transport industry sources said.

Truck drivers are not taking a direct role in the work stoppage, which so far only involves state employees, but fear of leftist guerrilla attacks and disruption by striking workers has kept many off the roads.

Julian Parra, commercial director of the influential Colombian Transport Federation (Colfecar), which represents transport companies and some truck drivers, blamed the government for whipping up paranoia in the lead-up to the strike.

"The government generated fear about the strike as part of its traditional discourse to undermine labor action," he said. "Road cargo was cut by between 20 percent and 30 percent Tuesday but people are beginning to regain confidence after they saw there were no great incidents of violence," he added.

Parra said traditional products such as flowers and coffee were among the most affected. But he said the situation was beginning to "get back to normal" Wednesday as cargo owners realized Tuesday that the threat against their goods was not as great as first thought.

John Naranjo, commercial manager of the National Coffee Growers' Federation, said Tuesday that the shipment of coffee to ports had been adversely affected by the public sector strike. He was unable to give an exact figure but said the flow of coffee cargoes to ports had been much lower than average.

Luis Fernando Ospina, executive director of the Association of Colombian Transport Workers, estimated road freight was down at least 30 percent because of the strike, which began midnight Monday (0500 GMT Tuesday).

The main factor keeping truck drivers off the roads was a warning issued Monday by the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second largest guerrilla group, he said, threatening to burn tractor-trailers while the state workers' action lasted, he said.
The ELN has frequently used the threat of a so-called "armed strike" to paralyze whole sections of the country.
